himera.t: The first Greek city on Sicily's north coast, site of the great Greek victory over Carthage in 480 BCE and destroyed by Carthage in revenge in 409 BCE.
himera.o: Settlers from Zancle, joined by exiles from Syracuse, founded Himera in 648 BCE at the mouth of the Himera river, on Sicily's northern coast. As the westernmost Greek city on that coast, it faced the Phoenician towns of Panormus and Soloeis and the Elymians.
himera.r: Himera spoke a mixture of Chalcidian and Doric Greek and was home to the poet Stesichorus. Its tyrant Terillus was expelled by Theron of Acragas around 483 BCE and appealed to Carthage. In 480 BCE Gelon of Syracuse and Theron crushed the Carthaginian army of Hamilcar outside the city, and the Victory Temple was built in thanks. Theron's son then governed Himera, and later it was a democracy.
himera.e: In 409 BCE Hannibal Mago, grandson of Hamilcar, took Himera, razed it and is said to have executed 3,000 prisoners on the spot where his grandfather had died. Survivors and Carthaginian settlers founded Thermae Himeraeae nearby in 407 BCE. The ruins and battlefield cemeteries have been excavated.

hirpini.t: Samnite people of the southern Apennines, named after the wolf that legend says led them, who resisted Rome until the Social War.
hirpini.o: The Hirpini lived in the mountains of modern Irpinia, east of Campania. Their name was explained from the Oscan word hirpus, 'wolf', after the animal that guided their ancestors in a 'sacred spring' migration from the Sabine lands. They were one of the peoples of the Samnite League.
hirpini.r: Their centres included Maleventum (later Beneventum), Aeclanum, Compsa and Abellinum. They lived from herding and farming in upland valleys, and the sanctuary of the goddess Mefitis in the Ansanto valley, by sulphurous springs, was a major cult site. As part of Samnium they fought Rome in the Samnite Wars.
hirpini.e: After the Samnite defeat Rome founded Beneventum on Hirpine land in 268 BCE. The Hirpini went over to Hannibal after Cannae and were punished. They joined the Italian revolt in 91 BCE; Sulla took Aeclanum in 89 BCE, after which they submitted and received citizenship.

high-kingship-of-ireland.t: The prestigious title of king of Tara and over-king of Ireland, contested for centuries by the Ui Neill and later by provincial dynasties such as Brian Boru's.
high-kingship-of-ireland.o: The kingship of Tara, an ancient royal site in Meath, was claimed from the 6th century by the Ui Neill dynasties, who presented it as an ancient kingship of all Ireland. Their northern and southern branches alternated the title for several centuries, though actual authority rarely reached beyond the northern half of the island.
high-kingship-of-ireland.r: The high king was an overlord rather than a ruler of a centralised state: he took hostages and tribute from provincial kings and held the Feis Temro and fairs. Monastic chroniclers and law tracts built up the ideology of a sacred kingship. Real power depended on military success.
high-kingship-of-ireland.e: Brian Boru of Munster broke the Ui Neill monopoly around 1002, and later kings ruled 'with opposition'. Ruaidri Ua Conchobair, the last high king, submitted to Henry II after the Norman invasion of 1171 and the Lordship of Ireland; he died in 1198.

hispania-ulterior.t: Rome's province of Further Spain, covering the rich south and west of Iberia from 197 BCE until Augustus split it into Baetica and Lusitania.
hispania-ulterior.o: After driving Carthage out of Iberia in 206 BCE, Rome first governed the conquered south through commanders. In 197 BCE it created two provinces, each under a praetor; Hispania Ulterior covered the Guadalquivir valley and the lands to the west, including Gades and the former territory of the Turdetani.
hispania-ulterior.r: Governors based at Corduba, founded by Marcus Claudius Marcellus in the 2nd century BCE, commanded armies and collected tribute from Iberian and Phoenician towns. Silver mining, oil and grain made it rich, while campaigns against the Lusitanians dominated the 2nd century BCE. Julius Caesar served there as quaestor and then governor in 61 BCE.
hispania-ulterior.e: In the civil wars it was a stronghold of the Pompeians, defeated by Caesar at Munda in 45 BCE. From 27 BCE Augustus reorganised it into Hispania Baetica and Lusitania, though the formal division took several years.

hispania-citerior.t: Rome's province of Nearer Spain, from the Ebro and the east coast into the Meseta, the base for Rome's long wars against the Celtiberians.
hispania-citerior.o: Hispania Citerior was created in 197 BCE as one of the two Roman provinces in Iberia, covering the Mediterranean coast from the Pyrenees to beyond Carthago Nova. It grew from Rome's wartime base at Tarraco, established after Gnaeus Scipio's landing in 218 BCE.
hispania-citerior.r: A praetor or consul governed from Tarraco or Carthago Nova, leading near-constant campaigns. Cato crushed the north-eastern revolt in 195 BCE, and Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus made treaties with the Celtiberians in 179 BCE. The silver mines around Carthago Nova were among the richest in the Roman world. The province steadily pushed inland, taking Numantia in 133 BCE.
hispania-citerior.e: It was the main theatre of Sertorius' war from 80 to 72 BCE, ended by Pompey, and of Caesar's victory at Ilerda in 49 BCE. In 27 BCE Augustus enlarged it as Hispania Tarraconensis, adding the north-west after the Cantabrian Wars.

helvii.t: Gallic people of the Vivarais who stayed loyal to Rome in 52 BCE and from whose land Caesar crossed the snowbound Cévennes.
helvii.o: The Helvii lived on the right bank of the Rhône in the modern Ardèche, at the edge of the Massif Central. Their land became part of the Roman Province after 121 BCE.
helvii.r: Caesar names their leading man, Gaius Valerius Caburus, who had received Roman citizenship, an early example of a Gallic noble family adopting Roman ways.
helvii.e: In 52 BCE the Helvii were attacked by the Gabali and Arverni for their loyalty. Caesar marched through their territory and crossed the Cévennes in deep snow to strike the Arverni. Their Roman town was Alba Helviorum (Alba-la-Romaine), and the region later became the Vivarais.

helvetii.t: Celtic confederation of the Swiss plateau whose attempted mass migration in 58 BCE triggered Caesar's conquest of Gaul.
helvetii.o: Tacitus says the Helvetii once lived between the Rhine and the Main before moving to the Swiss plateau between the Jura and the Alps. They were divided into four cantons, and one of them, the Tigurini under Divico, joined the Cimbri and defeated a Roman army near Agen in 107 BCE.
helvetii.r: They lived in fortified oppida and villages and were governed by a nobility. The site of La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel, with its weapons and offerings, has given its name to the late Iron Age culture of Celtic Europe.
helvetii.e: Led first by Orgetorix, they burned their towns and set off west in 58 BCE, but Caesar defeated them near Bibracte and sent the survivors home. Under Rome Aventicum (Avenches) became their capital, and modern Switzerland still calls itself Confoederatio Helvetica.

hipponion.t: Colony of Locri on the Tyrrhenian coast of Calabria, known for an Orphic gold tablet, which became the Roman colony of Vibo Valentia in 192 BCE.
hipponion.o: Locri Epizephyrii founded Hipponion in the 7th century BCE on a hill above the Gulf of Sant'Eufemia, giving the Locrians a port on the Tyrrhenian Sea and a share in the trade crossing the Calabrian isthmus.
hipponion.r: Hipponion depended on Locri for much of its history and shared its alliances. It had temples, a city wall and a port. A gold leaf found in a woman's grave of about 400 BCE gives Orphic instructions for the soul in the underworld and is a key text for Greek mystery religion.
hipponion.e: Dionysius I destroyed Hipponion in 389 BCE and moved its people to Syracuse, but Carthage restored them in 379 BCE. The Bruttii captured it around 356 BCE, and Agathocles briefly held it. Rome founded the Latin colony of Vibo Valentia there in 192 BCE, today's Vibo Valentia.

halicarnassus.t: Greek and Carian port city, birthplace of Herodotus and home of Queen Artemisia, which became the capital of Mausolus and the site of his Mausoleum.
halicarnassus.o: Halicarnassus was founded by Dorian settlers from Troezen on a bay of the Carian coast, beside native Carian communities, and the two populations mixed. It belonged to the Dorian Hexapolis but, according to Herodotus, was expelled after one of its citizens carried off a prize tripod.
halicarnassus.r: Under the Achaemenid Empire it was ruled by a Carian-Greek dynasty: Lygdamis I and his daughter Artemisia I, who commanded ships for Xerxes at Salamis in 480 BCE. Herodotus, born there, opposed Lygdamis II and went into exile. After the tyranny ended, Halicarnassus joined the Delian League.
halicarnassus.e: Mausolus of Hecatomnid Caria made Halicarnassus his capital in the 370s BCE, absorbing it into his dynastic state; his tomb, the Mausoleum, was a Wonder of the World. Alexander besieged the city in 334 BCE. It is modern Bodrum.

hellenic-alliance.t: The alliance of Greek states, led by Sparta, that defeated the invasion of Xerxes at Salamis, Plataea and Mycale in 480-479 BCE.
hellenic-alliance.o: In autumn 481 BCE, as the Persian king Xerxes gathered his army in Asia Minor, delegates of the Greek states willing to resist met at the Isthmus of Corinth. They swore an alliance, ended their own feuds, including the war between Athens and Aegina, and sent envoys to seek help from Argos, Syracuse, Corcyra and Crete, with little success.
hellenic-alliance.r: The alliance had a council of delegates (probouloi) meeting at the Isthmus, but command lay with Sparta, which led on land and, through Eurybiades, at sea, although Themistocles' Athenian fleet was the largest. Some 31 states are named on the Serpent Column dedicated at Delphi after the war. Members who had sided with Persia were threatened with punishment.
hellenic-alliance.e: After victories at Salamis (480 BCE) and Plataea and Mycale (479 BCE), the Greeks carried the war to the Aegean. The arrogance of the Spartan regent Pausanias at Byzantium in 478 BCE led the Ionian allies to turn to Athens, which founded the Delian League. The alliance itself lingered formally until 461 BCE.

heraclea-pontica.t: Powerful Greek city on the southern Black Sea coast, known for its serf-like Mariandynian subjects, its philosopher-tyrants and its own daughter colonies.
heraclea-pontica.o: Heraclea was founded c. 560 BCE by settlers from Megara joined by Boeotians, on the coast of north-west Anatolia where Heracles was said to have descended to the underworld. The colonists subdued the local Mariandynians, who became a dependent rural population compared by ancient writers to the helots of Sparta.
heraclea-pontica.r: Heraclea controlled a wide territory, a strong fleet and trade in grain, timber and nuts, and founded Chersonesus Taurica in Crimea. Its oligarchy gave way in 364 BCE to the tyranny of Clearchus, a former pupil of Plato and Isocrates, and his family. His widowed daughter-in-law Amastris ruled and later married Lysimachus. The local historian Memnon preserved its story.
heraclea-pontica.e: After the tyranny ended, Heraclea regained independence, allied with Rome and later with Mithridates VI of Pontus. In the Third Mithridatic War the Roman commander Marcus Aurelius Cotta took and sacked it in 70 BCE. It recovered under Roman rule and survives as the Turkish town of Karadeniz Eregli.
